The Narrow-nosed planigale (Planigale tenuirostris), one of Australia's smallest marsupials, exhibits an extraordinary life history for an animal of its minute body size. Females reach an ultimate body mass of just 4.3 grams [Wwi = 4.3 grams], while males are slightly heavier, attaining an adult weight of 4.5 grams [Wwi = 4.5 grams]. These values place it among the lightest of dasyurid carnivores. Based on an extrapolation from the larger eastern quoll (Dasyurus viverrinus), it is estimated that the wet weight at birth is a mere 0.0235 grams [Wwb = 0.0235 grams]. This minuscule neonatal mass reflects the extreme altriciality typical of the family, with newborn young being essentially embryonic in form and completing most of their development within the maternal pouch.

Under typical thermal conditions of 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C], which represents the species' active-phase body temperature, the gestation period lasts a mere 19 days [tg = 19 days]. This brief intrauterine development is consistent with the marsupial reproductive strategy of giving birth to highly underdeveloped neonates after a short gestation. The time since birth at weaning is 95 days [tx = 95 days] during this period, when the offspring transition from complete dependence on milk to consuming invertebrate prey. at a temperature of 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C]The high metabolic cost of lactation for such a diminutive mammal is substantial, as she must nearly double her own energetic intake to provision the rapidly growing litter.

Reproductive output is notably limited by the species' size and metabolic constraints. At 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C], females typically produce 6 pups per litter [N_R_i = 6 pups per litter], a relatively moderate litter size for a dasyurid of this scale. Litter production occurs twice per year [F_R_i = Litter production occurs twice per year] under these thermal conditions, allowing for a maximum annual reproductive rate of around 12 offspring. Full sexual maturation is a protracted process relative to the lifespan. Puberty, defined as the time since birth at which gonadal maturation completes, occurs at 240 days [tp = 240 days] when maintained at the species' normal body temperature of 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C]. This delayed maturation likely reflects the need for the animal to achieve sufficient body mass and fat reserves before undertaking the energetic demands of reproduction.

Longevity in Planigale tenuirostris is surprisingly extended given its diminutive size. Under laboratory conditions at a constant 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan spans approximately 5.2 years [am = approximately 5.2 years], translating to about 1,898 days. This lifespan is notably long for a mammal of under 5 grams, exceeding predictions based on body mass alone and aligning more closely with the patterns seen in other small dasyurids that exhibit semelparous or iteroparous strategies. The capacity to survive multiple breeding seasons is critical, as it permits females to invest in repeated litters over successive years, thereby compensating for the high juvenile mortality typical of such small-bodied insectivores in Australia's unpredictable environments.

The mass at which nutritional independence occurs provides insight into the growth trajectory. When young leave the pouch and cease suckling, they have attained a wet weight at weaning of 2.9 grams [Wwx = 2.9 grams], representing a dramatic increase from the birth mass of 0.0235 grams [Wwb = 0.0235 grams]. This nearly 125-fold increase in body mass is accomplished during the 95-day lactation period at 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C], with weaning occurring at 95 days after birth [tx = 95 days after birth]. The weanlings must then quickly learn to hunt small arthropods to sustain their own growth toward the adult mass of approximately 4.3 to 4.5 grams (4.3-4.5 grams) [Wwi = 4.3-4.5 grams], a final growth phase that demands efficient foraging in the leaf litter of their semi-arid grassland habitats.
